title: Algorithm Design Patterns: A Field Guide

questions.question: A ticket reads: 'flag any card with more than 5 transactions in any 10-minute window'. Before choosing an algorithm, which two facts most narrow the choice?
options: The database engine in use and the programming language the team writes
The input shape (a per-card event sequence) and the latency budget per event
The total number of cards on file and the official name of the fraud rule
Whether the team's style guide prefers recursive or iterative solutions
questions.explanation: Shape rules out graph and interval patterns at once, and a per-event budget of microseconds rules out anything that rescans the window. Together they point at a sliding window with incremental state. Language and engine are implementation choices made after the pattern is known.

questions.question: Which statement correctly pairs a pattern with the proof it owes before it can be called optimal?
options: Greedy owes a recurrence with base cases
Binary search on the answer owes an exchange argument
Dijkstra owes non-negative edge weights
Dynamic programming owes a monotone feasibility check
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's popped-node-is-final invariant holds only without negative edges. Greedy owes the exchange argument, DP owes the recurrence (optimal substructure), and binary search on the answer owes monotonicity; the other options swap these.

questions.question: A payout file must be split into the fewest batches under a per-batch cap. In which case is the one-pass greedy fill provably optimal, and in which is it a heuristic?
options: Optimal if the lines may be reordered; heuristic if order must be preserved
Optimal if order must be preserved; heuristic (bin packing) if lines may be reordered
Optimal in both cases, because capacity constraints always admit greedy
Heuristic in both cases, because batching is NP-hard
questions.explanation: With order fixed, delaying a batch boundary never hurts, which is the exchange argument. Allowing reordering makes it bin packing, NP-hard, where first-fit-decreasing is a heuristic with a known 11/9 bound. The constraint on order is what flips provable into heuristic.

questions.question: 'Find the cheapest THB-to-NGN conversion through available currency pairs.' Which tempting pattern is wrong here, and why?
options: Dijkstra, because currency graphs are always far too large for a heap-based search
Union-find, because it can only tell whether two currencies are connected, not through which pairs
Sliding window, because rates change over time and a trailing window would capture the drift
BFS, because it minimizes hops rather than cost and can return a two-hop route costlier than a three-hop one
questions.explanation: BFS treats every edge as cost 1; the problem has weighted edges (spreads), so the fewest-hop path is not the cheapest. Dijkstra on -log(rate) weights is the right tool, with Bellman-Ford if any rate exceeds 1 after spread. Union-find does answer connectivity, just not cost.

questions.question: 'Smallest per-job timeout such that 99.9% of yesterday's jobs would have finished.' Which pattern is the most direct, and what does the binary-search-on-the-answer view add?
options: Quickselect for the 99.9th percentile in O(n); the binary-search view shows the answer is unique since the fraction finishing within X is monotone in X
Sort every duration; binary search adds nothing because once sorted the data is already ordered by X
Dynamic programming over job durations in minor units; binary search is used only to size the table before filling it
A heap of all durations popped 0.1% of the way; binary search locates the heap index at which to stop popping
questions.explanation: The answer is an order statistic, so selection finds it in linear time without a sort. Seeing the problem as 'minimum X such that a monotone check passes' is what guarantees a unique answer exists and would let you binary search if the data were only available through a counting query. DP and heaps do not fit the shape.

questions.question: In the Cloudflare (2019) and Stack Overflow (2016) outages, what was the shared recognition failure?
options: Using a hash map for lookups where a sorted array with binary search was the required structure
Running Dijkstra on a currency graph with negative edges so that the shortest path returned was silently wrong
Sampling the first N requests of each day instead of drawing a uniform reservoir sample across the whole stream
Choosing a backtracking regex engine for a matching task without asking its cost per unit of input, when a linear-time approach existed
questions.explanation: Both incidents were quadratic regex behaviour on long inputs: a WAF rule and a whitespace trim. The fixes were a linear-time matching engine and a hand-written O(n) loop. The miss was not skill but skipping the input-size and cost-per-unit questions before reaching for the familiar tool.
